title: Longest Mountain in an Array

concept.title: Expand from each peak
body: A **mountain** is a block with at least 3 elements that strictly increases up to a peak and then strictly decreases. Find a peak first (`a[i-1] < a[i] > a[i+1]`), then walk left while the values keep decreasing, and right while they keep decreasing. The mountain is everything between.

body.code:
if a[i-1] < a[i] > a[i+1]:
    l = i - 1
    while l > 0 and a[l-1] < a[l]: l -= 1
    r = i + 1
    while r < n - 1 and a[r] > a[r+1]: r += 1
    best = max(best, r - l + 1)
    i = r        # nothing before r can start another peak

body: Jumping `i` to the end of the mountain makes every element visited a constant number of times, so the whole scan is O(n) although there are loops inside the loop.

statement: A **mountain** is a block of at least 3 consecutive elements that strictly increases up to one element (the peak) and then strictly decreases. Print the length of the longest mountain in the array, or 0 if there is none.
hints: A peak is an element that is greater than both neighbours.
From a peak, walk left while the values decrease and right while they decrease.
The mountain length is `right - left + 1`. Continue after the right end.

explanation: Every mountain has exactly one peak. Expand from each peak to both sides and skip to the end of the mountain, so no element is scanned many times.

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n = int(input())
a = list(map(int, input().split()))

best = 0
i = 1
while i < n - 1:
    if a[i - 1] < a[i] and a[i] > a[i + 1]:
        l = i - 1
        while l > 0 and a[l - 1] < a[l]:
            l -= 1
        rr = i + 1
        while rr < n - 1 and a[rr] > a[rr + 1]:
            rr += 1
        best = max(best, rr - l + 1)
        i = rr
    else:
        i += 1
print(best)
